claim: Targeted sequencing of sixteen SLE risk loci among 1349 Caucasian cases and controls produced a comprehensive dataset of the variations causing susceptibility to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: Targeted sequencing of sixteen SLE risk loci among 1349 Caucasian cases and controls produced a comprehensive dataset of the variations causing susceptibility to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
evidence: The manuscript describes the targeted sequencing study performed on 1349 samples (773 cases and 576 controls) as documented in the methods and results sections.

claim: Two independent disease association signals in the HLA-D region identified two regulatory regions containing 3562 polymorphisms that modified thirty-seven transcription factor binding sites.
source: Two independent disease association signals in the HLA-D region identified two regulatory regions containing 3562 polymorphisms that modified thirty-seven transcription factor binding sites.
evidence: The manuscript presents sequencing data and ENCODE annotations identifying these polymorphisms and their effects on transcription factor binding sites.

claim: Variations modifying the consensus binding motifs of IRF4 and CTCF in the XL9 regulatory complex modified the transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1 in a chromosome-specific manner.
source: Variations modifying the consensus binding motifs of IRF4 and CTCF in the XL9 regulatory complex modified the transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1 in a chromosome-specific manner
evidence: The manuscript presents allele-specific transcription data in heterozygous individuals showing chromosome-specific effects (Figure 6E).

claim: SLE risk genotypes result in a 2.5-fold increase in the surface expression of HLA-DR and DQ molecules on dendritic cells.
source: resulting in a 2.5-fold increase in the surface expression of HLA-DR and DQ molecules on dendritic cells with SLE risk genotypes
evidence: Flow cytometry data presented in Figure 7 demonstrates increased surface expression of HLA-DR and HLA-DQ on dendritic cells from individuals with risk genotypes.

claim: After stimulation, the increase in HLA-DR and DQ surface expression on dendritic cells with SLE risk genotypes increases to over 4-fold.
source: which increases to over 4-fold after stimulation
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 7 shows increased expression after TLR7/8 stimulation.

claim: Common disease alleles contain multiple causal variants modulating multiple immune system genes.
source: demonstrated that common disease alleles contain multiple causal variants modulating multiple immune system genes
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing 1206 functional variants across 16 loci affecting multiple genes (Table 1).

claim: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease resulting from a profound loss of immune tolerance to self-antigens.
source: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease resulting from a profound loss of immune tolerance to self-antigens
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature (Olsen and Karp, 2014; Theofilopoulos, 1995a; 1995b; Fairhurst et al., 2006).

claim: SLE disease pathology begins with the deposition of immune complexes in various target tissues, leading to the activation of inflammatory effector mechanisms that damage critical organ systems.
source: Disease pathology begins with the deposition of immune complexes in various target tissues, leading to the activation of inflammatory effector mechanisms that damage critical organ systems.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about SLE pathogenesis.

claim: SLE patients typically produce autoantibodies against more than 10 different self-antigens.
source: The disease initiates with the production of autoantibodies against a spectrum of self-antigens (typically >10 in SLE patients)
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic feature of SLE and is consistent with established clinical knowledge.

claim: More than 50 SLE risk loci have been identified by genome-wide association analyses (GWAS).
source: Genome-wide association analyses (GWAS) have identified more than 50 SLE risk loci to date
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to GWAS studies (Harley et al., 2009; Nath et al., 2008; Harley et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2012; Graham et al., 2006; 2008; 2009; Hom et al., 2008; Gateva et al., 2009; Relle et al., 2015).

claim: Targeted genomic sequencing of twenty-eight GWAS-confirmed SLE risk loci was performed using Illumina custom enrichment arrays on genomic DNA from 1775 SLE patients and controls.
source: Targeted genomic sequencing of twenty-eight GWAS-confirmed SLE risk loci was performed using Illumina (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA) custom enrichment arrays on genomic DNA from 1775 SLE patients and controls
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methodology used in the study.

claim: The sequencing study identified 124,552 high quality sequence variants contained in 28 risk loci among 1349 Caucasian cases (773) and controls (576).
source: Our sequencing study identified 124,552 high quality sequence variants contained in these risk loci among 1349 Caucasian cases (773) and controls (576).
evidence: This is a direct result from the sequencing analysis as described in the methods and results.

claim: Multiple SLE risk haplotypes within the HLA-D region coordinately upregulate HLA-DR, -DQ and a variety of other genes within the antigen processing and presentation pathways for HLA class I and class II molecules.
source: multiple SLE risk haplotypes within the HLA-D region were found to coordinately upregulate HLA-DR, -DQ and a variety of other genes within the antigen processing and presentation pathways for HLA class I and class II molecules
evidence: This is supported by eQTL analysis and expression data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The custom enrichment array theoretically captured sequence information for ~99.94% of the ~4.4 Mbs of genome targeted in these risk loci.
source: The Illumina custom enrichment system theoretically captured sequence information for ~99.94% of the ~4.4 Mbs of genome targeted in these risk loci.
evidence: This is a specification of the enrichment array design.

claim: Target enrichment was highly specific and efficient, typically resulting in >70% of reads on target and resulting in >128X average coverage for the 28 risk loci analyzed.
source: target enrichment was highly specific and efficient, typically resulting in >70% of reads on target and resulting in >128X average coverage for the 28 risk loci analyzed
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1B showing sequencing coverage metrics.

claim: Continuous sequences could be derived for >85% of the targeted intervals in assembled sequences.
source: continuous sequences could be derived for >85% of the targeted intervals in assembled sequences
evidence: This describes the quality of sequence assembly achieved in the study.

claim: The final dataset included 114,487 single nucleotide variations (SNVs) and 10,065 insertion/deletion (In/Del) polymorphisms.
source: 124,552 high quality variants, of which 114,487 are single nucleotide variations (SNVs) and 10,065 are insertion/deletion (In/Del) polymorphisms
evidence: This is a summary of the variant calling results after quality filtering.

claim: The concordance of sequence-based SNV calls versus SNV calls with the Illumina Immunochip was >99.8% for samples with >25X average coverage.
source: the concordance of sequence-based SNV calls versus SNV calls with the Illumina Immunochip was >99.8% for samples with >25X average coverage
evidence: This validation is shown in Figure 1G comparing sequencing and Immunochip genotyping.

claim: The sequence-based variant database identifies an average of one variant every 39 basepairs through 4.4 Mb of genomic DNA in 28 validated SLE risk loci.
source: This sequence-based variant database, which identifies an average of one variant every 39 basepairs through 4.4 Mb of genomic DNA in 28 validated SLE risk loci
evidence: This is calculated from the total number of variants (124,552) divided by the total genomic region sequenced (4.4 Mb).

claim: The sequence analyses identified 70070 previously annotated variations and 54482 unannotated or novel variations.
source: Our sequence analyses identified 70070 previously annotated variations and 54482 unannotated or novel variations.
evidence: This is shown in the variant annotation analysis presented in Figure 2B,C.

claim: About 40% of the variants in the dataset were potentially functional.
source: Functional annotation determined that about 40% of the variants in the dataset were potentially functional
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B demonstrating the proportion of functional variants.

claim: Most potentially functional variants were categorized as regulatory based on their localization into ENCODE-defined regulatory segments or inclusion in eQTL datasets.
source: most of which were categorized as regulatory based on their localization into ENCODE-defined regulatory segments or inclusion in eQTL datasets
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing the distribution of variant types.

claim: Sixteen risk loci were selected for detailed analyses based predominantly on the presence of multiple variations showing strong associations with disease.
source: Sixteen risk loci were selected for more detailed analyses, based predominantly on the presence of multiple variations showing strong associations with disease.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for detailed analysis as shown in Table 1.

claim: Conditional analyses identified four risk loci with multiple, independent signals: NMNAT2-SMG7, TNFSF4, HLA-D, and XKR6.
source: conditional analyses identified four risk loci with multiple, independent signals. This indicates that NMNAT2-SMG7, TNFSF4, HLA-D, and XKR6 each contained two or more LD blocks
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and the conditional analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: 1206 functionally annotated variants were in tight LD (D'>0.8) with the 21 peak risk signals.
source: 1206 functionally annotated variants were in tight LD (D'>0.8) with the 21 peak risk signals
evidence: This is tabulated in Table 1 showing the total number of functional variants across all analyzed loci.

claim: All but 7 of the 1206 functionally annotated variants in tight LD with peak signals were non-coding, regulatory variants.
source: all but 7 of these were non-coding, regulatory variants
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 which lists coding and total functional variants for each locus.

claim: Multiple functional variations are in tight LD with the peak disease associated signal in every risk locus.
source: These results demonstrate that multiple functional variations are in tight LD with the peak disease associated signal in every risk locus.
evidence: This is demonstrated across all 16 loci analyzed as shown in Table 1 and Figures 4-13.

claim: The STAT4 risk locus contains nine potentially functional SLE associated variants that form six haplotypes.
source: Figure 4D presents the patterns of sequence divergence that distinguish these haplotypes
evidence: Figure 4D-E shows the LD structure and haplotype analysis for STAT4.

claim: STAT4 HAP2 is strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (OR 1.7, p<4.8 × 10-9).
source: HAP2 (highlighted in red) from the haplotypes in the protective clade
evidence: Figure 4E shows the haplotype association statistics for STAT4.

claim: SNP2 (rs11889341) in STAT4 is strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (p<4.8 × 10-9) and impacts the transcription levels of STAT1 and STAT4.
source: SNP2 (rs11889341) is the most potent of several eQTL variants within the STAT4 risk locus is very strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (p<4.8 × 10-9), and impacts the transcription levels of STAT1 and STAT4
evidence: Figure 4G shows eQTL effects of SNP2 on STAT1 and STAT4 expression in macrophages.

claim: The T allele of SNP2 (rs11889341) in STAT4 is associated with increased baseline STAT1 and STAT4 transcription and associates with susceptibility to SLE.
source: our eQTL dataset for monocyte-derived macrophages (MDM) identifies a significant increase in baseline STAT1 and STAT4 transcription with the T allele of SNP2, which associates this phenotype with susceptibility to SLE
evidence: Figure 4G presents the eQTL data showing increased expression with the T allele.

claim: Sequence analysis of the HLA-D region revealed 15129 common variants distributed throughout the 448 Kb segment analyzed.
source: Sequence analysis of the HLA-D region revealed 15129 common variants (1 variant/29.6 bp) distributed throughout the 448 Kb segment analyzed.
evidence: This is a direct result from the sequencing analysis of the HLA-D region.

claim: More common (15129) than rare (12076) variants were detected in HLA-D, which differs significantly from the roughly 5-fold excess of rare variants typically detected throughout the human genome.
source: More common (15129) than rare (12076) variants were detected in HLA-D, which differs significantly from the roughly 5-fold excess of rare variants that are typically detected throughout the human genome and at other SLE risk loci in our study
evidence: This is supported by comparison to data from the 1000 Genomes Project (Abecasis et al., 2010; 2012; Hu et al., 2014) and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The preponderance of common variants in the HLA-D sequence dataset is consistent with an ancient origin of these HLA-D polymorphisms within the human lineage.
source: The preponderance of common variants in this sequence dataset is consistent with an ancient origin of these HLA-D polymorphisms within the human lineage.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the variant frequency data and is supported by citations to studies on MHC evolution (McConnell et al., 1988; Lawlor et al., 1988; Gyllensten and Erlich, 1989; Edwards et al., 1997; She and Wakeland, 1991).

claim: The LD structure of HLA-D variations in the EA cohort is very similar to the LD structure obtained for this segment of HLA-D in the 2504 human genomes in the 1000 genome project.
source: the LD structure of these HLA-D variations in our EA cohort is very similar to the LD structure obtained for this segment of HLA-D in the 2504 human genomes in the 1000 genome project
evidence: Figure 5Ai and ii show the comparison of LD structures between the study cohort and 1000 Genomes data.

claim: 3786 variations in HLA-D are nominally associated with SLE (p<0.05).
source: 3786 variations in HLA-D are nominally associated with SLE (p<0.05)
evidence: This is a result from the association analysis of HLA-D variants.

claim: 1797 of the SLE-associated HLA-D variants have annotated regulatory functions.
source: 1797 of these have annotated regulatory functions
evidence: This is shown in the annotation analysis of HLA-D variants as illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Five separate segments within HLA-D contained variants achieving genome-wide significance for association with SLE.
source: Five separate segments within HLA-D contained variants achieving genome-wide significance for association with SLE.
evidence: Figure 5B shows the Manhattan plot with five distinct association peaks in HLA-D.

claim: The peak SLE association in HLA-D was with rs9271593 (p=6.50E-10), which is one of 687 SLE-associated regulatory variants mapping to the XL9 regulatory component.
source: The peak SLE association was with rs9271593 (p=6.50E-10), which is one of 687 SLE-associated regulatory variants mapping to the XL9 regulatory component within the intergenic region separating DRB1 and DQA1
evidence: This is shown in the association analysis results and Table 1.

claim: The XL9 segment of HLA-D is not adequately covered by SNP typing arrays such as the Immunochip v.1.
source: the XL9 segment of HLA-D is not adequately covered by SNP typing arrays such as the Immunochip v.1, possibly accounting for the failure to detect this potent SLE association in previous GWAS analyses
evidence: Figure 5Aiii & iv shows the sparse SNP coverage in XL9 on the Immunochip compared to the sequencing data.

claim: The second strongest SLE association signal in HLA-D was with rs9274678 (p=6.21E-09), which is located in a segment extending 5' from the DQB1 proximal promoter.
source: The second strongest SLE association signal was with rs9274678 (p=6.21E-09), which is located in a segment extending 5' from the DQB1 proximal promoter.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: The third genome-wide SLE signal in HLA-D was with rs36101847 (p=8.33E-09), which is located in close proximity to DRB1 exon 2.
source: The third genome-wide SLE signal was with rs36101847 (p=8.33E-09), which has no functional annotation and is located in close proximity to DRB1 exon 2
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: Conditional analysis identified three independent disease associations in HLA-D, each localized to important regulatory or coding elements.
source: these conditional analyses identified three independent disease associations, each localized to important regulatory or coding elements within HLA-D
evidence: Figure 5B shows the conditional analysis removing associations sequentially.

claim: Conditioning on the XL9 signal (rs9271593) completely removed the SLE association of variants within the DRB1 to DQA1 intergenic segment.
source: conditioning on the XL9 signal (rs9271593) completely removed the SLE association of variants within the DRB1 to DQA1 intergenic segment
evidence: Figure 5C shows the conditional analysis results for the XL9 region.

claim: 56 functional variants in the XL9 region with strong ENCODE functional effect scores, eQTL effects, and associations with SLE formed 12 haplotypes.
source: This identified 56 functional variants that formed 12 haplotypes
evidence: Figure 5D,E shows the LD structure and haplotype analysis for XL9.

claim: XL9 HAP3 was strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (OR 2.0, p<7.04 E-08).
source: HAP3 was strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (OR 2.0, p<7.04 E-08)
evidence: Figure 5E shows the haplotype association statistics for XL9.

claim: XL9 HAP1 (OR 0.58, p<1.63 E -06) and HAP6 (OR 0.34, p<1.69 E-07) were protective against SLE.
source: while HAP1 (OR 0.58, p<1.63 E -06) and HAP6 (OR 0.34, p<1.69 E-07) were protective
evidence: Figure 5E shows the haplotype association statistics for XL9.

claim: MJ analysis found that the protective and risk XL9 haplotypes form separate clades at opposite ends of the network.
source: MJ analysis found that the protective (shaded in blue) and risk (shaded in red) haplotypes form separate clades at opposite ends of the network
evidence: Figure 5F shows the median-joining network for XL9 haplotypes.

claim: XL9 contains binding sites for multiple factors affecting chromatin structure (CTCF, ZNF143) and has been shown to assemble HLA-DR and HLA–DQ proximal promoters into a transcriptional complex.
source: XL9 contains binding sites for multiple factors affecting chromatin structure (CTCF, ZNF143) and has been shown to assemble HLA-DR and HLA–DQ proximal promoters into a transcriptional complex that facilitates coordinate, tissue-specific transcription
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Bailey et al., 2015; Xi et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2008; Whitfield et al., 2012).

claim: IRF4 up-regulation of MHC class II molecules was shown to be strongly associated with disease severity in a murine model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
source: IRF4 up-regulation of MHC class II molecules was shown by these investigators to be strongly associated with disease severity in a murine model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)
evidence: This is cited from the work of Singh and co-workers (Vander Lugt et al., 2014).

claim: A 1 Kb segment in the center of XL9 contains more than 30 transcription and chromatin configuration factor binding sites.
source: This segment contains more than 30 transcription and chromatin configuration factor binding sites.
evidence: Figure 6B shows the fine map of this XL9 segment with binding sites annotated.

claim: Thirteen of the fifty-six potent regulatory variants in the XL9 haplotypes are located within a 1 Kb segment in the center of XL9.
source: Thirteen of the fifty-six potent regulatory variants in the XL9 haplotypes are located within this small segment.
evidence: Figure 6B shows the locations of these variants within the XL9 segment.

claim: Five variants in the XL9 1 Kb segment are located in the consensus binding sites for CTCF, ZNF143, or IRF4 and are predicted to impact their binding properties.
source: Five of these variants are located in the consensus binding sites for CTCF, ZNF143, or IRF4 and are predicted to impact their binding properties
evidence: Figure 6B shows the locations of these variants within transcription factor binding motifs.

claim: For both IRF4 variants in XL9, alleles carrying the unmodified IRF4 consensus binding sequence are associated with the risk haplotypes.
source: For both of these variants, alleles carrying the unmodified IRF4 consensus binding sequence are associated with the risk haplotypes, while those with nucleotides that are less common to the consensus motif are present in all of the non-risk haplotypes
evidence: Figure 5F, Figure 6C, and Supplementary file 2 show the association of IRF4 consensus sequences with risk haplotypes.

claim: The HAP2 and HAP3 alleles of XL9 variants are strongly associated with increased transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 in MDM cell cultures.
source: the HAP2 and HAP3 alleles of variants within this short segment, including an IRF4 motif variant, are strongly associated with increased transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 in our eQTL panel of MDM cell cultures
evidence: Figure 6D shows the eQTL effects of XL9 variants on HLA class II gene expression.

claim: XL9 regulatory variations modulate the level of transcription of HLA-DR and HLA-DQ in a chromosome-specific manner.
source: these experiments demonstrate that XL9 regulatory variations modulate the level of transcription of HLA-DR and HLA-DQ in a chromosome-specific manner
evidence: Figure 6E shows allele-specific transcription data in heterozygous individuals.

claim: Coding region variants linked with XL9 risk associated regulatory variants are present in a significantly higher proportion of RNA-SEQ reads than coding variants linked to protective alleles.
source: coding region variants linked with XL9 risk associated regulatory variants are present in a significantly higher proportion of RNA-SEQ reads than coding variants linked to protective alleles
evidence: Figure 6E shows the allelic bias in RNA-seq read depth for HLA class II genes.

claim: Individuals homozygous for XL9 HAP3 (risk) variations have more than two-fold higher surface expression for HLA-DR and DQ molecules at baseline than HAP1 (protective) homozygotes on monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
source: individuals homozygous for XL9 HAP3 (risk) variations have more than two-fold higher surface expression for HLA-DR and DQ molecules at baseline which increases to 4-fold after stimulation with TLR-ligand on monocyte-derived dendritic cells than HAP1 (protective) homozygotes

claim: After stimulation with TLR-ligand, the difference in HLA-DR and DQ surface expression between XL9 HAP3 and HAP1 homozygotes increases to 4-fold on monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
source: which increases to 4-fold after stimulation with TLR-ligand on monocyte-derived dendritic cells

claim: None of the DQB1 5' regulatory variants are correlated with eQTL effects that impact DQB1, although they are associated with transcriptional effects on other genes within the antigen processing pathway of HLA.
source: none of the regulatory variants are correlated with eQTL effects that impact DQB1, although they are associated with transcriptional effects on other genes within the antigen processing pathway of HLA, such as PSMB8, PSMB9, TAP1, TAP2, DQA2, and DQB2

claim: DQB1 5' HAP4 was protective (OR 0.3, p<3.88 E-09) and HAP2 condoned risk (OR 1.9, p<1.11 E-06).
source: HAP4 was protective (OR 0.3, p<3.88 E-09) and HAP2 condoned risk (OR 1.9, p<1.11 E-06)

claim: The DRB1 signal is associated with twenty eight regulatory variations distributed from the peak SNP through DRB1 and about 10 Kb 5' from the DRB1 start site.
source: The DRB1 regulatory variants are distributed in a region extending from the peak SNP through DRB1 and about 10 Kb 5' from the DRB1 start site towards the XL9 regulatory region.

claim: DRB1 HAP6 is protective (OR 0.4, p=4.58E-05) and HAP1 is risk (OR 1.6, p=1.50E-06).
source: HAP6 is protective (OR 0.4, p=4.58E-05) and HAP1 is risk (OR 1.6, p=1.50E-06)

claim: HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 class II alleles were imputed with four digit accuracy for the EA cohort using the sequence data.
source: The HLA-D sequence data allowed the imputation of standard HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 class II alleles with four digit accuracy for the EA cohort

source: XL9 regulatory polymorphisms can completely remove the associations of HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQA1 imputation variants with SLE

source: These analyses indicate that variations in XL9 and HLA-DRB1 class II alleles are in tight LD and represent a combined contribution to SLE

claim: Variations in the segment 5' of DQB1 independently contribute to SLE susceptibility.
source: while variations in the segment 5' of DQB1 independently contribute to SLE susceptibility

source: all homozygotes for regulatory HAP3 (peak risk) are also homozygous for DRB1_0301, DQA1_0501, DQB1_0201, which is the HLA-D class II haplotype found in the extended DR3 haplotype

claim: Peak risk haplotypes result in an overall 17% increase in the average odds ratio for the sixteen loci tested compared to GWAS tagging SNPs.
source: resulting in an overall 17% increase in the average odds ratio for the sixteen loci tested

claim: The increase in odds ratio achieved by identifying peak risk haplotypes is consistent with theoretical predictions of identifying causative variants in complex disease risk loci.
source: This result is consistent with theoretical predictions of the increase in odds ratio that would be achieved by specifically identifying causative variants in complex disease risk loci, thus supporting the presence of the causal variants of SLE within the identified functional haplotypes

claim: Six or fewer haplotypes account for about 90% of the LD block regulatory sequences segregating in the EA population at individual risk loci.
